title: Client Connector as a forwarding method: benefits, limits and Z-Tunnel modes

prose.text: Client Connector is the method that follows the user. {{remote-users}} {{benefits}}

prose.label: Costs and prerequisites.
prose.text: {{limitations}} {{requirements}} The old reference said every forwarding method ends as a Location; for this one the vendor describes the app connecting 'from an unknown location' ([[zia.locations.model]] has the Road Warrior tag for such traffic).

prose.label: Tunnel modes.
prose.text: {{z-tunnel-1}} {{z-tunnel-2}} {{z-tunnel-2-single-ip-nat}} The mechanism and bypass design are in [[zcc.z-tunnel]] and [[zcc.forwarding-profiles]]. Which proxy mode each tunnel mode corresponds to is in [[zia.proxy-mode.forwarding-map]]; how a site's GRE egress can trigger the fallback is in [[zia.traffic-forwarding.mixed-deployments]].
Whether trusted-network detection defers to a GRE tunnel is open {{gap:zcc-covers-gre-fallback}}.

remote-users.statement: Zscaler recommends Client Connector on user devices to protect web traffic from an unknown location (a remote user): the app detects when the user leaves the secure network and creates a connection to the service from an unknown location.

quotes: Zscaler recommends that you install Zscaler Client Connector on your users' devices to protect their web traffic when they are accessing the internet from an unknown location (i.e., remote user).
then automatically creates a connection to the Zscaler service from an unknown location.

benefits.statement: Client Connector covers Windows, macOS, Linux, iOS, Android and virtual desktops, supports every authentication mechanism the service supports, fingerprints devices, detects trusted networks and can disable itself there, forwards all ports and protocols, can be prevented from being disabled or uninstalled, and supports SSL Inspection for its users.

quotes: Supports Windows, macOS, Linux, iOS, Android, and virtual computing environments.
Supports all authentication mechanisms supported by the Zscaler service.
Detects trusted networks and can disable its service automatically.
Zscaler Client Connector forwards traffic for all ports and protocols to the Zscaler service for inspection from any location
Zscaler Client Connector can be configured to prevent your users from disabling, bypassing, or uninstalling it.
You can deploy SSL Inspection for Zscaler Client Connector users.

limitations.statement: Where a public IP is mapped to the user's location, some location-based policies (Firewall, Forwarding Control, DNS) apply to the user's Client Connector traffic, but the vendor says Sublocations, Surrogate IP and Bandwidth Control "cannot be enabled for your organization", and the software must be deployed, managed and maintained on every device.

quotes: Client Connector traffic.Features such as Sublocations, Surrogate IP, and Bandwidth Control cannot be enabled for your organization.A software application needs to be deployed, managed, and maintained on all end devices.

requirements.statement: Users must be provisioned and have an authentication method configured; Private Access through the app requires SAML authentication, and the firewall must allow the connections the app needs for internet security.

quotes: The Zscaler Client Connector users must be provisioned on the Zscaler service and an authentication method must be configured for them to authenticate.
If you are using the app for Private Access (ZPA), your organization must use SAML authentication.
If you are using the app for internet security, your firewall must be configured to allow the necessary connections.

z-tunnel-1.statement: Z-Tunnel 1.0 forwards traffic by CONNECT requests, like a traditional proxy, sending all proxy-aware traffic or port 80/443 traffic depending on the forwarding profile; it is selected in a forwarding profile in Tunnel mode with the packet filter driver enabled.

quotes: Z-Tunnel 1.0 forwards traffic to the Zscaler cloud via CONNECT requests, much like a traditional proxy.
Z-Tunnel 1.0 sends all proxy-aware traffic or port 80/443 traffic to the Zscaler service, depending on the forwarding profile configuration.
To use Z-Tunnel 1.0, select Z-Tunnel 1.0 when configuring a forwarding profile with Tunnel mode and the packet filter driver is enabled.

z-tunnel-2.statement: Z-Tunnel 2.0 sends packets over DTLS or TLS and can carry all ports and protocols; using it means deploying a supported Client Connector version, selecting Z-Tunnel 2.0 in a Tunnel-mode forwarding profile with the packet filter driver enabled, and configuring bypasses in App Profiles.

quotes: Z-Tunnel 2.0 has a tunneling architecture that uses DTLS or TLS to send packets to the Zscaler service. Because of this, Z-Tunnel 2.0 is capable of sending all ports and protocols.
Configure bypasses for Z-Tunnel 2.0 in App Profiles.

z-tunnel-2-single-ip-nat.statement: Z-Tunnel 2.0 needs a NAT device that uses a single IP for all connections from one device; otherwise control and data connections can land on different Service Edges, Z-Tunnel 2.0 fails to establish and the client falls back to Z-Tunnel 1.0.

quotes: For Z-Tunnel 2.0, use a NAT device that uses a single IP for all connections from a single device.
Z-Tunnel 2.0 fails to establish and falls back to Z-Tunnel 1.0.

zcc-covers-gre-fallback.title: Client Connector as a second layer behind tunnels
zcc-covers-gre-fallback.detail: Unverified legacy statement: On-network users are covered by GRE or IPSec but Client Connector provides a second-layer fallback, and on trusted networks it may defer to GRE. No captured source states it; operator experience or a tenant observation would settle it.
